extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law scholars, legal academics, and policymakers interested in democratic theory and regulatory institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how well administrative institutions (e.g., notice-and-comment, negotiated rulemaking, agency design, interagency coordination) realize democratic aims such as deliberation, representativeness, accountability, and public justification amid polarization and inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public justification / seeking support
rubrics_metrics.description: By aspiring to win others’ support, one is seeking to rule with them, not over them. And by making claims openly justiﬁable to those potentially bound by them, one is going beyond self-interest to orient oneself to a common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic legitimacy requires that decisions be openly justifiable to those potentially bound by them; institutions should foster processes where rulers seek to win support rather than impose rule. (Quoted normative standard framing classical democratic theory.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to generate consensus/deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical theories see democratic administration as a method for settling conﬂicts so government decisions represent the will of the dêmos; institutions should reduce conﬂict and promote consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether procedural and institutional designs (notice-and-comment, deliberative forums, negotiated rulemaking) actually produce public-minded deliberation synthesizing disparate preferences, especially in contexts of deep value conflict. The piece notes that extreme polarization and inequality make such consensus unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of notice-and-comment participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment procedures are valuable for the opportunity for agency-public deliberation, but most participation consists of form comments—simple expressions of support or opposition that commenters view as a 'vote'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comment content (substantive argument vs form support/opposition), not just volume. Agencies should consider whether comments facilitate deliberation or merely register preferences; mass form comments are less deliberatively valuable. The discussion cites scholarship on form comments and debates whether agencies should 'count' mass comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness of participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal equality of opportunity to comment does not ensure representative participation; those with systemic advantages (industry, well-heeled orgs) dominate, while marginalized perspectives are underrepresented or absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether the snapshot of views during comment periods reflects a representative cross-section of affected communities. Consider empirical evidence (e.g., financial-rulemaking research) showing skew toward organized interests and the underrepresentation of marginalized groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity/authenticity of comments (fraud/mass campaigns)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rise of mass-commenting campaigns and notice-and-comment fraud (computer-generated, fraudulent comments) burdens the process and raises questions about whether and how agencies should treat such comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mechanisms to detect and handle bot-generated or fraudulent comments, and weigh positions about whether mass comments should 'count' at all. Cite ACUS manuscript and literature on fraudulent or malattributed comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to change entrenched political preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment rulemaking seems incapable of reducing conﬂict in highly politicized domains because political preferences (e.g., DACA) are baked into political identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether participatory procedures can realistically alter deep partisan commitments; use case studies (DHS/DACA) showing little change in public support despite notice-and-comment processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of procedural innovations to improve inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural innovations (electronic interfaces, dynamic comment periods, other reforms) have generally failed to stoke higher-quality commenting or to rectify inequalities in participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing technological or procedural reforms, require empirical evidence they increase substantive participation by marginalized groups and improve comment quality, not merely aggregate counts. Cite literature (Coglianese, Cortland & Tani, Widman) showing limited success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness and legitimacy of negotiated rulemaking and advisory committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiated rulemaking and FACA advisory committees aim to produce consensus via stakeholder representation, but negotiating committees are often unrepresentative and FACA processes can be politicized or used to leverage outside constituencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate composition and selection of participants for representativeness, the likelihood of producing durable consensus, and the risk of politicization; consider empirical findings that negotiated rules still face litigation and that advisory committees may be staffed to support partisan initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural cost-benefit and 'procedure fetish'
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures are not costless; layering on more participatory procedures should be tempered by honest assessment of what they can deliver. Administrative-law scholars often have a 'procedure fetish.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require cost-benefit reasoning before adding procedural layers: analyze administrative costs, delay, potential improvements in legitimacy or outcomes, and whether added procedures will actually address the democratic deficits identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to Weberian bureaucracy (clarity and accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Weberian ideal (rigid hierarchies, uniform goals, internal absence of conflict) is the implicit benchmark for grounding democratic accountability through political control; the American administrative state is sprawling, parochial, competitive, and fragmented rather than Weberian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether agencies exhibit clear lines of authority, coherent ends-means rationality, and manageable goal ambiguity; fragmentation undermines the capacity to hold agencies democratically accountable via elected officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lines of political accountability to elected officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic legitimacy grounded in 'accountability' requires a bureaucracy resembling the Weberian model so elected officials can control outputs; scholars look to mechanisms like OIRA centralized review and presidential direction to supply this accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the clarity and effectiveness of formal accountability channels (presidential control, congressional oversight, OIRA coordination) and whether they reliably align agency outputs with electoral preferences without producing undue concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desirability and democratic implications of institutional fragmentation/adversarialism
rubrics_metrics.description: Some scholars defend institutional fragmentation and adversarial interagency relations as productive friction that improves regulatory outcomes, constrains abuse, and responds to complexity; but these are not straightforwardly democratic defenses under conventional theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When valuing fragmentation, weigh instrumental benefits (innovation, checks on power) against democratic costs (harder to locate electoral accountability, potential appeal of unitary executive). The article calls for a democratic theory able to tolerate agonistic fragmentation if it is to be normatively justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of plebiscitary presidentialism when democratic grounding fails
rubrics_metrics.description: If existing theories cannot defend fragmentation and people continue to expect democratic accountability from agencies, presidential populism and unitary-executive claims become appealing, opening the door to plebiscitary authoritarianism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional designs for their ability to prevent slide toward plebiscitary or authoritarian remedies: consider whether reforms strengthen distributed democratic checks or inadvertently increase attractiveness of unitary presidential control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a democratic theory tolerant of agonistic conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Missing from pro-conﬂict accounts is a democratic theory that can tolerate, if not embrace, internal fragmentation and conﬂict for democratic reasons rather than merely instrumental ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional reforms and procedural designs against whether they are supported by a coherent democratic theory that legitimates agonistic, plural, or adversarial administrative structures, rather than relying solely on pragmatic or instrumental justifications.
